I'd like to feed in a sequence of inputs and print which state we end in, following the matching transition for each input step by step.

# Edge-Owned Lifetime P1 — engineering design v4 (twice red-teamed, FINAL)

**Author: CEO seat, 2026-07-10. Supersedes v1/v2/v3.**
Vetting history: v1 red-teamed by a 27-agent panel (6 archetypes + Q-adjudicator + per-finding verifiers;
run `wf_afc06c8c`): 30 raw → 19 unique → **16 survived (3 FATAL, 7 MAJOR), 3 refuted** — all folded into v3.
v3's two post-panel elements (the fulfilled/revoked asymmetry + the C5 sweep) got a focused 3-lens pass
(run `wf_ed7d8894`): verdicts SOUND-WITH-FIXES ×2, UNSOUND ×1 — the UNSOUND was earned (an immortal
answered-then-churning zombie + a sweep clause that violated the invariant it claimed to enforce), and all
its findings are folded here (marked **[v3-Fn]**). One v3-pass claim was itself refuted by direct code
check: `insert_child_session` DOES hardcode `archive_when_idle=TRUE` (`db/queries/sessions.py:316-326`,
literal `TRUE` in the VALUES) — every edge-created child of either creator carries the flag, which is what
makes the clause structure below sufficient. Companion to `architecture/edge-owned-lifetime.md` (the
primitive; amended per §1 here). File:line references verified against `eumemic/aios` master `133c090e`.

## §1 The invariant

**A lease-bound node holds a lease per open inbound awaited edge. Revocation of its last lease tears it
down immediately and revokes its own open outbound awaited edges, recursively. Fulfillment of its last
lease buys graceful reclaim at idle PLUS a bounded churn allowance (the lease ceiling) — not immortality.**

**[v3-F1, the honest correction — FATAL in both lenses]:** v3's absolute ("fulfilled closures always take
the graceful idle path; nothing forceful ever follows a fulfilled edge") created a structurally immortal
state: a servicer that answers its ask and then keeps churning on self-generated tool stimuli is never
revocable (first-writer-wins), never idle (`session_active_predicate` stays true on its own tool loop), and
was reachable by no sweep clause — the 2026-07-09 incident class re-opened one generation down. Worse, v3's
C5 clause 1 silently compensated by force-archiving *fulfilled* children of terminal runs, violating the
stated invariant. v4 resolves the contradiction by making the bound explicit: **graceful gets first shot
(idle-reclaim, any time); the lease ceiling is the activity-blind backstop that no never-idle node can
dodge.** The M3 protection survives in bounded form: a busy servicer that honored its ask finishes its
tail work if it idles within the ceiling window; an ephemeral-flagged session churning past the ceiling
with zero open leases is by definition the runaway class.

This issue integrates, but does not reopen or replace, the accepted decisions in #2-#14 and ADR-0001-ADR-0008.

**Normative acceptance annexes:**

1. [Core contract and 14-state lifecycle matrix](https://github.com/Lijika/xiaopeng_comp/issues/16#issuecomment-5150838279).
2. [S01-S17 delivery-slice matrix](https://github.com/Lijika/xiaopeng_comp/issues/16#issuecomment-5150838454).
3. [A01-A14 migration/retirement matrix](https://github.com/Lijika/xiaopeng_comp/issues/16#issuecomment-5150838611).

The body plus those three comments form one specification. A row is complete only when every named evidence field and its release gate pass; prose, unit tests, screenshots, historical regressions, or reused code alone cannot satisfy a row.

## Problem Statement

Automotive-finance reviewers need one accountable place to determine whether the documents and field evidence within an application are mutually consistent, resolve uncertainty without overwriting machine conclusions, and hand a verification route to the separate disbursement-approval process. The current MVP demonstrates selected normalization, matching, rules, reports, adapters, and synthetic regressions, but its flat `Application -> RuleEngine -> Report` path has no authoritative application lifecycle, immutable evidence history, governed release, role-separated human decisions, durable concurrency/recovery semantics, or formal evaluation plane. Treating it as the product would lose provenance and overstate security and performance.

Current evidence also cannot support a real cross-document performance claim. There are 21 real motor-vehicle registration certificates and 97 images; Step2 covers 10 samples/44 page records, and OCR-derived artifacts cover 10 samples/40 actually processed pages. There is no real same-application multi-document corpus or independent ground truth. The 159 synthetic applications and 1,920 visible label pairs are development regressions, not an acceptance holdout.

## Solution

Build a **Consistency Review Workbench** whose unit of work and audit is one application. A registered source submits a versioned canonical envelope; the workbench atomically admits valid facts into an immutable evidence graph, derives one lifecycle-owned current state, freezes evidence and one governed policy release into each check run, and routes mandatory findings to automatic completion or accountable human work. Reviewers work from a queue into a finding-first, dual-pane application workspace; they can verify uncertainty, append corrections, request supplements, or request a separately approved exception. The workbench emits a verification route and durable downstream-delivery obligation, never a loan approval or rejection.

The target is a modular-monolith control plane with independent workers and an isolated evaluation runner. PostgreSQL owns structured facts, institution-controlled object storage owns attachments and large immutable artifacts, and all external surfaces are adapters around typed commands, immutable references, and minimized query DTOs. Public competition demonstration and controlled deployment share a pure domain/checking core but have separate identities, data, storage, networks, credentials, audit, and deployment manifests.

Issue #98: Complete real-device, accessibility, responsive, and performance qualification

## Business outcome
Deliver complete real-device, accessibility, responsive, and performance qualification as a reviewable end-to-end first-release slice.

## In scope
Physical Android/iOS, desktop/mobile-web, connectivity/permissions, screen readers/large text and latency/query/bundle thresholds.

## Out of scope
Adjacent later slices, general ledger/payroll, and autonomous decisions.

## Domain terminology
Real Device, Pending Sync, accessibility, performance evidence.

## Dependencies
Parent #62. Blocked by #97.

## Authorization and approval rules
Server capabilities and relevant Company/Branch/Warehouse/assignment scope apply; financial/quantity limits and Maker-Checker apply to sensitive approvals; administrators do not auto-approve.

## Immutable stock or financial effects
No direct balance edits. Any stock or financial effect is an immutable source-linked movement/entry; corrections are linked reversals/replacements. Read/capture-only slices explicitly produce no posting until their posting command.

## Idempotency and concurrency
Mutations require stable idempotency keys/responses and expected versions; serialize at the source document plus affected customer, receipt, line, identity or SKU/Warehouse grain; outbox handlers are committed and idempotent.

## API, database, worker, web, and mobile impact
Infrastructure, CI/CD, migration/recovery tooling, observability, web/mobile builds, runbooks and evidence. Implement the smallest cohesive portion described in scope.

## Acceptance scenarios
- Happy path and required partial states pass.
- Missing capability, cross-scope, self-approval/over-limit and stale state are denied where applicable.
- response-loss retry and concurrent commands create exactly one valid effect set.
- rollback leaves no partial state.
- responsive/offline/native behavior matches PRD allocation.

## Migration requirements
Add only required tables/constraints/indexes/immutable triggers; verify upgrade, downgrade, and re-upgrade with deterministic backfill.

## Projection rebuild and reconciliation
Delete/rebuild applicable projections from immutable sources; reconcile exact counts, quantities, values, balances, states, document links and effect identities.

## Testing expectations
Implement the slice first, then add focused risk-based contract tests; cover DB invariants, authorization, limits, idempotency, concurrency, rollback, outbox/retry, migration, generated-client, desktop/mobile-web and native/offline paths where assigned.

## Documentation and release gates
Update applicable context/ADR/architecture/testing docs, OpenAPI and generated client when contracts change, release notes, and checkpoint. Run focused tests and all repository gates; complete independent standards/specification reviews with no unresolved P1/P2; publish a draft PR and do not merge without explicit approval.

## Feature-specific acceptance scenarios

- Critical journeys pass on physical Android/iOS and desktop/mobile-web under poor connectivity/denied permissions.
- WCAG 2.2 AA and documented latency/query/bundle thresholds pass or have owned accepted risk.

Issue #17: [Task] Host Health Execution, Caching, and Scoped Dependencies

## Summary

Extend the AuthKit host health infrastructure to execute plugin health checks safely and efficiently, and to cache their results for a configurable TTL.

The host must create dedicated dependency injection scope for each health check execution and measure health check execution latency. Latency is **host observed execution metadata** and must not be placed inside `PluginHealthResult.Data`, which stays plugin owned diagnostic metadata (see D5–D6). To keep the plugin contract clean, the host wraps the plugin result together with the measured duration in a **host-side** execution result, and caches that wrapper.

## Goal

Provide production safe host side execution of the structured plugin health contract introduced in D1–D6.

The implementation must ensure that:

- plugin health checks execute within scoped `IServiceProvider`,
- scoped dependencies are disposed correctly (including async disposal),
- health check execution latency is measured by the host,
- the measured latency is exposed through a host-side wrapper, never inside plugin `Data`,
- repeated health requests do not unnecessarily execute expensive plugin checks,
- cached results expire according to a defined TTL,
- and cancellation is propagated correctly.

## Background

Plugin health checks may depend on scoped services such as:
```text
Database contexts
Repositories
External service clients
Transactions
Other scoped dependencies
```
Resolving these services directly from the root `IServiceProvider` can cause lifetime violations, dependency resolution errors, or resource leaks.

Health endpoints may also be polled frequently by:
```text
Load balancers
Kubernetes probes
Monitoring systems
Reverse proxies
Service discovery
```
Executing every plugin health check on every request can therefore generate unnecessary database, network, and other dependency traffic.

The host should cache completed health executions for configurable TTL while still allowing health information to expire and refresh.

Finally, health check latency should be measured by the host rather than requiring every plugin to implement its own timing logic.

## Scope

### D7. Host Side Health Check Execution

The host must execute each plugin health check inside dedicated DI scope and measure its execution duration.

To keep the plugin contract unchanged, the host introduces **host side** result type that wraps the plugin's `PluginHealthResult` together with the measured duration:
```csharp
public sealed record PluginHealthExecutionResult(
    IReadOnlyCollection<PluginHealthResult> Results,
    TimeSpan Duration);
```

D7 covers:

1. create the DI scope,
2. resolve the scoped dependencies required by the health check,
3. execute the health check (honoring `CancellationToken` from D4),
4. measure the execution duration (host-side),
5. dispose the scope (including async disposal),
6. build `PluginHealthExecutionResult(Results, Duration)`,
7. propagate exceptions and cancellation explicitly.

`PluginHealthResult.Data` remains **plugin owned diagnostic metadata**. Host latency is never written into `Data`.

### D8. Health Result Caching

The host must cache completed health executions for configurable TTL.

The cache stores the **host side** execution wrapper together with its expiration, not bare `PluginHealthResult`:
```csharp
internal sealed record CachedPluginHealthExecution(
    IReadOnlyCollection<PluginHealthResult> Results,
    TimeSpan Duration,
    DateTimeOffset ExpiresAt);
```

D8 covers:

1. cache the completed `PluginHealthExecutionResult` as `CachedPluginHealthExecution`,
2. associate the cache entry with the correct plugin/health context (cache keys),
3. expire entries according to the TTL,
4. support explicit cache disabling,
5. de-duplicate concurrent refreshes (single flight),
6. keep concurrent access thread safe,
7. never cache an incomplete/cancelled execution as valid result.

The implementation must not resolve scoped plugin dependencies directly from the root service

Issue #4116: [build] fluss-filesystems uber-jars ship unshaded jackson + guava that can shadow downstream dependencies

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched in the [issues](https://github.com/apache/fluss/issues) and found nothing similar.


### Fluss version

main (development)

### Please describe the bug 🐞

While fixing the same class of shading leak in `fluss-fs-s3` (#4073, follow-up to  
#3884), I checked the rest of the `fluss-filesystems` family. I rebuilt every fs  
plugin from current `main` and inspected the produced shaded uber-jar. **All  
seven ship unshaded `com.fasterxml` (jackson) and `com.google` (guava)** that  
will shadow any downstream application's own jackson / guava on the classpath,  
causing `NoSuchMethodError` / `NoClassDefFoundError` / silent version skew — the  
same failure mode reported in #3884.

### Measured leak (top-level unshaded entries in the shaded uber-jar)

| Plugin         | jackson (`com/fasterxml`) | guava (`com/google`) | MRJ escaped* | notes                                                                              |
| -------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| fluss-fs-hdfs  | **1,073**                 | **2,731**            | 25           | baseline                                                                           |
| fluss-fs-s3    | **1,093**                 | **2,042**            | 25           | leaks on `main`; fix proposed in open PR #4073 (not yet merged)                    |
| fluss-fs-oss   | **1,073**                 | **2,230**            | 25           |                                                                                    |
| fluss-fs-cos   | **1,073**                 | **2,246**            | 25           |                                                                                    |
| fluss-fs-azure | **1,073**                 | **2,042**            | 25           |                                                                                    |
| fluss-fs-obs   | **1,161**                 | **2,042**            | 25           |                                                                                    |
| fluss-fs-gs    | **1,073**                 | **7,351**            | 25           | **worst**: ~3.6× the guava of the others, and no relocated copy at all (see below) |

\* MRJ = `META-INF/versions/N/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/io/doubleparser/**`  
entries that escape relocation — the exact #3884 bug class, present in all 7.

`fluss-fs-hadoop-shaded` is **not** fine either: as @binary-signal noted in the discussion, it relocates `com.fasterxml` → `org.apache.fluss.fs.shaded.hadoop3.com.fasterxml` correctly and does ship hadoop's guava as `org.apache.hadoop.thirdparty.com.google` (third-partied by hadoop), but it **also** ships its own **unshaded** guava (1,954 `com.google.common`) and commons (2,228 `org.apache.commons`). Those leak into every consumer fs plugin that bundles it — which is part of why the guava counts in the table above run as high as they do. Tracked in #4143, fixed in #4144.

A maintainer on the project paiml/forjar (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #368: apply --plan-file never prompts before a destructive change, and that is call-graph shape rather than a decision

`forjar apply` prompts before executing a destructive change. `forjar apply --plan-file p.json` does not — with or without `--yes`. The prompt is not suppressed on that path; it is never reached.

Found while deciding what every `ApplyConfig` field should do on the `--plan-file` path (#358).

## Where it goes missing

The confirmation lives in `src/cli/apply_preflight.rs:99`:

```rust
if confirm_destructive && !dry_run && !yes {
```

reached from the ordinary apply path. `src/cli/apply_from_plan.rs` — the whole `--plan-file` branch — contains no reference to `confirm_destructive`, to `apply_preflight`, or to any prompt. `dispatch_apply_b.rs` returns into `cmd_apply_from_plan` before the preflight that would raise it.

So a plan whose body carries `to_destroy > 0` is executed without asking, on a terminal where a plain `apply` of the same delta would stop and wait.

## Is that wrong?

Arguably not, and that is why this is an issue rather than a patch. Two defensible readings:

**It is correct.** `--plan-file` executes a *reviewed* delta. The operator has already seen `to_destroy: 3` in the plan output; prompting again asks them to re-confirm a decision they made deliberately, which is how confirmation fatigue starts. This is the Terraform posture: `terraform apply tfplan` does not prompt, precisely because the plan was the approval step.

**It is wrong.** The prompt is not only about surprise, it is about *elapsed time and provenance*. A plan file can be minutes or days old, can arrive from CI, and — as #358 established — is not authenticated: an unkeyed seal means anyone who can run `forjar plan` can produce one. A destroy is the one action whose cost is unrecoverable, and the human at the terminal may not be the human who reviewed the plan.

The epic's own F-MCP-002 spec assumed the second reading: it specifies `destroy_confirmed: true` as mandatory when `to_destroy > 0`, failing with `DESTRUCTION_NOT_CONFIRMED` otherwise.

## What is not defensible either way

The current state is neither posture on purpose — the prompt is absent because of call-graph shape, not because anyone chose it. Nothing documents it, `--yes` implies there is something to skip, and an operator who has learned that `apply` asks before destroying will reasonably assume `apply --plan-file` does too.

## Suggested resolution

Decide, then make the decision visible:

- If plan applies should not prompt, say so in `--plan-file`'s help text and in the book, and note that the plan output IS the confirmation step.
- If they should, route the plan path through the same preflight, and let `--yes` skip it as it does elsewhere. A middle option worth considering: prompt only when the plan is older than some threshold, since the "already reviewed" argument weakens with age — though forjar has no trusted clock (see the TTL discussion in #358), so wall-clock age is itself unreliable.

## Falsification test

A plan carrying a destroy, applied on a TTY without `--yes`: assert the documented behaviour, whichever is chosen. Today there is no assertion either way, which is how it went unnoticed.

Issue #76611: Matrix crypto-store: state only persisted on 60s timer + sync stop helpers do not await final persist (E2EE decryption breaks across restarts)

## Summary

Two related defects in the Matrix crypto-store persistence lifecycle that together can cause an OpenClaw Matrix bot to silently lose its ability to decrypt inbound E2EE messages over restart cycles, even with a fully-bootstrapped recovery key, server-side key backup, and verified cross-signing.

### Defect A — Crypto state is only persisted on a 60s timer

`initializeCryptoIfNeeded` schedules `setInterval(() => persistIdbToDisk(...), MATRIX_IDB_PERSIST_INTERVAL_MS)` (default 60s) and provides no event-driven flush in addition. When the rust crypto SDK establishes a new Olm session, decrypts an incoming Megolm key, finishes a key backup restore, or completes cross-signing rehydration, that state lives only in fake-indexeddb in process memory until the next 60s tick.

If the process exits inside that window (npm update, crash, OOM, manual restart), the just-negotiated Olm session is lost. The peer's Element keeps encrypting outbound to-device events with the same Olm session key the bot no longer has, producing repeating `InvalidMAC(MacError)` errors and "Established new Olm sessions" loops on the same `sender_key` until manual recovery (key request, reverify, or backup-restore CLI) is run.

### Defect B — Some shared-client stop APIs start final persistence but do not await it

`MatrixClient.stop()` correctly initiates final persistence (writes `syncStore.markCleanShutdown()`, kicks off `persistIdbToDisk` + `syncStore.flush()`, stores the resulting promise as `this.stopPersistPromise`; `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/sdk.ts:666-694`). `stopAndPersist()` awaits that promise.

However, the **synchronous** shared-client stop helpers do not:

- `stopSharedClient()` (`shared.ts:268-273`)
- `stopSharedClientForAccount()` (`shared.ts:275-282`)
- `stopSharedClientInstance()` (`shared.ts:294-299`)

All three call `client.stop()` and return `void`. They start the final persist promise but do not give callers a way to await it. The `releaseSharedClientInstance(..., "persist")` path (`shared.ts:301-322`) does correctly `await client.stopAndPersist()`, and the monitor cleanup path uses it (`monitor/index.ts:243`), so monitor-driven shutdowns are clean. Other call sites (e.g. one-off CLI flows, abort cleanup) using the synchronous variants can return before the persistence promise resolves.

### Combined effect

Defect A means recently-acquired keys are not yet on disk. Defect B means whichever shutdown path uses the synchronous helpers does not wait for the in-flight final persist. Together, this is the slow-burn E2EE-decryption-broken pattern.

## Symptom (observed in practice)

After enough restart cycles where the synchronous stop path is taken or the process exits before the 60s tick:

- `bot-storage.json` contains `"cleanShutdown": false`
- Logs show `[MatrixClient] WARN matrix_sdk_crypto::olm::account: Failed to decrypt a non-pre-key message with all available sessions ... InvalidMAC(MacError)`
- Followed by `[MatrixClient] INFO matrix_sdk_crypto::session_manager::sessions: Established new Olm sessions` for the same `sender_key`
- Loop repeats until manual intervention (reverify, key request, backup restore CLI)

A maintainer on the project SeCherkasov/SkerrySSH (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #306: SFTP transfer: the tree walk is unbounded, and the StackOverflowError it produces escapes the transfer's error handling

## What happens

`DownloadWalk.walk` / `UploadWalk.walk` in `composeApp/src/commonMain/kotlin/app/skerry/ui/files/TransferPlan.kt` recurse once per directory level with no depth cap, no visited set and no cap on the plan size:

```kotlin
FileItemType.Directory -> {
    plan.dirs += localPath
    sftp.list(remotePath).forEach { child ->
        walk(child.name, childPath(remotePath, child.name), child.type.toItemType(), child.size, localPath)
    }
}
```

If the remote tree loops — a bind mount that contains itself, a FUSE mount, or a hostile SFTP server that simply lists a directory as its own child — the walk never terminates. It grows `plan.dirs`/`plan.files` until the heap gives out, or blows the JVM stack first, whichever comes first.

Symlinks are not the vector: `FileItemType.Symlink` is skipped. Directory-typed loops are.

## Why it is worse than a hang

`buildDownloadPlan` is called from `runDownload` inside `TransferCoordinator.launchExclusive`, whose handler is:

```kotlin
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    transfers.end(TransferStatus.Failed(FileTransferFailure.Transfer)); throw e
} catch (e: Exception) {
    val failure = (e as? FileBrowserException)?.failure?.toTransferFailure() ?: FileTransferFailure.Transfer
    transfers.end(TransferStatus.Failed(failure))
} finally { onFinally(); busy = false }
```

`StackOverflowError` is an `Error`, not an `Exception`, so it matches neither clause. `transfers.end` is never called and the queue keeps an entry that stays Active forever; the `finally` clears `busy`, so the UI accepts a new transfer while the old one is still shown as running. `OutOfMemoryError` behaves the same way.

The whole plan is also built before the first byte moves, so even a legitimately huge tree gives an Active entry with no progress for as long as the walk takes.

## Expected

- Bound the walk: a maximum depth, a cap on the number of entries in a plan, or both — and fail with a typed `FileBrowserFailure` when exceeded, the way `isUnsafeListingName` already fails on a bad name.
- Widen the `launchExclusive` handler so a `Throwable` that is not `CancellationException` still ends the queue entry as Failed instead of leaving it Active.

## Repro

A maintainer on the project google-gemini/gemini-cli (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #29076: security(extensions): extension name path traversal allows write outside extensions directory

## Overview

A path traversal vulnerability exists in the gemini-cli extension installation flow (verified at upstream `main` commit `812f7a2bc`). Extension names taken from `extension.json` are used directly as filesystem path components, allowing a malicious extension to write files outside the intended `~/.gemini/extensions` directory.

## Vulnerable Code

In `packages/cli/src/config/extension-manager.ts` (lines 1266-1272) and `packages/cli/src/config/extensions/storage.ts`:

```ts
const extensionPath = path.join(extensionsDir, extensionName);
await fs.promises.cp(source, extensionPath, { recursive: true });
```

An extension.json containing:

```json
{
  "name": "../.config/autostart",
  "version": "1.0.0"
}
```

causes `gemini extensions install` or auto-update to write to `~/.config/autostart` or other sensitive locations.

## Root Causes

- `validateName` (regex `/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]+$/`) exists but is only applied in `inferInstallMetadata` for GitHub sources — not for local filesystem sources or when `extension.json` is manually crafted.
- `copyExtension` uses `fs.promises.cp` with `recursive: true` without verifying that `source` is within expected bounds.
- `makeWritableRecursive` follows symlinks without limit, enabling symlink attacks to overwrite arbitrary files.

## Repro Steps

1. Create a local extension dir with `extension.json` containing `{"name": "../evil", "version": "1.0.0"}`
2. Run `gemini extensions install /path/to/evil-extension`
3. Observe files written to the parent directory of the extensions dir

## Expected Fix

- Strictly validate `extensionName` against path traversal (`..`, `/`, `\`) at all entry points, not just GitHub inference, with explicit rejection if `path.join(extensionsDir, name)` resolves outside `extensionsDir` (via an `isWithinRoot` check).
- `copyExtension` should verify `source` is within the expected temp directory and `destination` is within the extensions directory before copying.
- `makeWritableRecursive` should limit symlink depth and not follow symlinks that escape the destination.

## Affected Scope

- Files: `packages/cli/src/config/extension-manager.ts`, `packages/cli/src/config/extensions/storage.ts`, `packages/cli/src/config/extension.ts`
- Affects all platforms; a malicious extension (e.g., from a compromised git repository) is the attack vector.

Issue #683: security: atomically reserve miner bundle root before packaging writes

## Overview

Security hardening for `l1/scripts/package-miner.mjs` (issue #683). The script currently removes the per-platform bundle path and then recreates descendants via recursive pathname-based `mkdir()` before copying/writing release files. An external filesystem actor able to replace the bundle path between cleanup and the first descendant creation/write — with a symlink/junction or different filesystem object — can redirect package materialization outside the canonical `miner-release` root.

This is distinct from #636 (which covers destination-directory identity during `copyMinerRuntimeTree()` traversal); this finding covers the top-level package bundle root used by all earlier/later `cp`, `writeFile`, `chmod`, and runtime-copy operations.

## Required behavior

- After cleanup, reserve the exact per-platform bundle root with non-recursive exclusive creation under the already-bound canonical `miner-release` root; fail closed if the path appears concurrently.
- Verify the newly created bundle is a real directory whose canonical parent remains the bound release root before any child directory creation, copy, chmod, or write.
- Do not follow a raced bundle-root symlink/junction.
- Preserve the existing canonical release-root boundary, the #636 nested destination-directory stop-ship, runtime source/destination custody, checksum publication, and signing/provenance/immutable-release/public-mining gates.
- Add deterministic regressions for a raced bundle-root symlink/junction and a pre-existing conflicting filesystem object, proving no external sentinel is modified.
- Add aligned miner-release security documentation.

## Merge gate

Use a separate agent branch/PR. Do not merge until the fixed expected head SHA has green general ZyronChain CI, Standalone L1 Node 22/24, Miner Package, Miner Release Candidate, and every other applicable required gate. This is release-candidate integrity hardening only — not public-mining/testnet/mainnet readiness evidence.

## Audit findings (comments by zyron249)

- **Staging+rename approach rejected.** After main `430800247f37b3ddac0b1e846056a7192c35a849`, an approach staging the entire bundle under a fresh random directory and atomically renaming it to the final bundle was evaluated. It prevents the final bundle leaf from being a write target, but only moves the same pathname-replacement window to the staging directory: subsequent `cp`/`writeFile`/`chmod` operations remain pathname-based, so an actor able to replace that directory can redirect writes before any post-check. This does not satisfy the issue's no-outside-write acceptance boundary; a staging-only pseudo-fix will not be merged and the gate will not be weakened. Branch `agent/miner-bundle-staging-publication-v1` is left clean for a future handle-relative/native directory primitive solution.
- **Post-#730 audit.** On main `cbb94f41fdb7ece2aeea1fe65bf41b5ff9a372f0`, the script still does `rm(bundle)` followed by pathname-based recursive `mkdir(join(bundle, ...))`, then pathname `cp`, `writeFile`, `chmod`, and runtime-tree writes. A non-recursive exclusive top-level `mkdir(bundle)` plus pre/post `lstat`/`realpath` narrows but does not eliminate the race — the bundle directory can still be replaced after validation and before any later child pathname operation. The acceptance boundary is not being weakened to detect-after-write. A complete fix needs a handle-relative/dirfd-style destination operation boundary (or an equivalently strong cross-platform abstraction) preventing raced parent replacement from redirecting child writes.
- **Repository search.** After main `60f19c925024ef5becf82c8155f1ebde266d1351`, a search found no existing `openat`/`dirfd`/`O_NOFOLLOW`/`CreateFileW`/`FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT` helper or equivalent descriptor-relative cross-platform write primitive. Pre/post `lstat`/`realpath` checks cannot prove the required raced-replacement property ("no bytes outside release root"). A valid fix requires an atomic/bound destination primitive plus deterministic race regressions before Miner Package/Release Candidate gates can count this as resolved.
- **Prerequisite.** `bindMinerReleaseRoot()` currently returns only a canonical pathname and does not retain stable release-root identity/handle across package materialization; tracked as #757. #757 is a prerequisite containment boundary for this issue: do not close #683 with a pathname-only `mkdir + lstat/realpath` change that narrows but does not eliminate the replacement race. #683 remains independently required for the per-platform bundle root once the parent-root custody model is sound.

## Current implementation

`l1/scripts/package-miner.mjs` performs top-level bundle cleanup (`rm(bundle)`), then pathname-based recursive `mkdir(join(bundle, ...))`, then pathname-based `cp`, `writeFile`, `chmod`, and runtime-tree writes — all vulnerable to raced bundle-path replacement.

Issue #1161: 🙋 [Feature] Add bounded SitemapReader for recursive, filtered knowledge ingestion

## Overview

Add a bounded **`SitemapReader`** to agentUniverse that ingests standard XML sitemaps and sitemap indexes into the knowledge pipeline, with optional page-content loading via the existing `WebPageReader` or an injected Reader. It understands the Sitemap protocol (URL sets, sitemap indexes, optional `lastmod`/`changefreq`/`priority` metadata, gzip-compressed files, up to 50,000 URLs / 50 MB per sitemap per spec) while enforcing much smaller configurable application bounds by default.

References: https://www.sitemaps.org/protocol.html, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap. Implementation: PR #1182.

## Motivation

agentUniverse currently has readers for one static page, one rendered page, and recursive HTML-link crawling, but cannot use a site's explicit sitemap inventory. For RAG ingestion:

- link crawling misses orphaned or weakly linked pages;
- navigation/footer crawling introduces duplicates and irrelevant URLs;
- sitemap metadata supports incremental refresh and provenance;
- large sites split URLs across nested sitemap indexes and gzip-compressed files;
- unbounded crawling is unsafe for library users and CI.

Duplicate review (Aug 15, 2026): checked `upstream/master`, all 403 open PRs via GitHub API, and searches for `sitemap`, `sitemap reader`, `RSS`, `Atom`, `feed reader` — no equivalent feature found. `XmlSplitter` (PR #827) processes XML only after loading; it does not discover URLs, recurse indexes, decompress, filter, or fetch page content.

## Use Cases

```python
reader = SitemapReader(
    max_urls=100,
    max_sitemaps=20,
    max_depth=3,
    max_sitemap_bytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
    request_timeout=20,
    max_redirects=5,
    max_workers=4,
)

documents = reader.load_data(
    sitemap_url="https://docs.example.com/sitemap.xml",
    load_content=True,
    include_patterns=[r"/guide/", r"/reference/"],
    exclude_patterns=[r"/archive/"],
    modified_since="2026-01-01",
)
```

- **Inventory mode** (`load_content=False`): one lightweight `Document` per selected URL, no page fetching. Metadata: URL/source, source sitemap, traversal depth, optional `lastmod`/`changefreq`/`priority`, `content_loaded: false`.
- **Content mode** (`load_content=True`): delegates each URL to `WebPageReader` or injected Reader, preserves result order, merges sitemap provenance into copied page documents. Per-page failures are summarized (`continue_on_error=True`) or raised (`False`).

Safety and correctness:
1. Accept only absolute HTTP(S) sitemap and page URLs; reject credentials in URLs.
2. Bound URLs, sitemap files, recursion depth, compressed/decompressed response size, redirects/timeouts, worker count.
3. Parse namespace-qualified and namespace-free `urlset` / `sitemapindex` XML.
4. Detect gzip by magic bytes, content type, or `.gz` suffix, including transparently decoded HTTP responses.
5. Detect cycles and deduplicate page URLs while preserving source order.
6. Restrict nested sitemaps and pages to the root origin by default.
7. Apply include/exclude regexes and `modified_since` (ISO-8601) before page fetching.
8. Do not mutate configured defaults when call overrides are supplied.
9. Do not hide malformed XML, invalid configuration, or root-sitemap failures.
10. Require no live network in unit tests.
11. Reject DTD/entity declarations; do not fabricate content on partial failures.

- [x] Recursively parse sitemap indexes within `max_depth` / `max_sitemaps`.
- [x] Support bounded gzip decompression and pre-decoded gzip responses.
- [x] Enforce URL, count, size, redirect, timeout, origin, and worker limits.
- [x] Deduplicate cyclic sitemap indexes and repeated page URLs.
- [x] Filter by include/exclude patterns and ISO-8601 `modified_since`.
- [x] Support inventory-only and delegated page-content modes.
- [x] Merge sitemap provenance without overwriting the page Reader's `source` metadata.
- [x] Provide deterministic partial-error summaries and fail-fast mode.
- [x] Validate request configuration before network work.
- [x] Provide component YAML, English docs, Chinese docs, and Reader index links.
- [x] Comprehensive offline tests: **55 passed**.
- [x] Pass Ruff, compileall, and `git diff --check`.
- [x] Local real-HTTP smoke test with a sitemap index and gzip child sitemap.

- `agentuniverse/agent/action/knowledge/reader/web/sitemap_reader.py`
- `sitemap_reader.yaml` registration
- Comprehensive offline tests

- No new mandatory dependency (`httpx` and standard library only)

- Bypassing robots policy.
- Recurring refresh scheduling.
- RSS/Atom parsing.
- Fetching beyond explicit configured bounds.

Issue #256: Inline diff review pane with anchored observations and read-only agent Q&A

## Overview

Add a TUI review pane over a selected commit's diff in pi. The diff is presented not in file order but as an ordered sequence of semantic change units following control flow, each annotated with the agent's own record of why the change was made. The user highlights a line, writes a review observation anchored to it, and asks the orchestrator a question about that line from inside the same thread. The agent answers; it never edits code.

## Use Cases

- Pick a commit from recent history and view its diff with syntax highlighting.
- Attach a free-text observation to a specific line (old side or new side).
- Observations persist across session reload and are deliverable to the agent.
- Per-line Q&A thread — user asks, orchestrator answers, no mutation.
- Present the commit as flow-ordered semantic units with agent narration, so the reviewer reads the change as a story instead of reconstructing the order manually.

## Non-goals

- Any agent action triggered from the pane. Q&A is strictly read-only.
- Replacing pi's chat — threads supplement the message stream.
- Multi-user / remote review. Local, single-developer, in-terminal.
- Editing code in the pane.
- Stacked commits; granularity stays one commit, only the presentation is chaptered.
- Full commit untangling as a research contribution — reuse existing partitioning.

## Decisions taken

### D1 — Stay in the TUI; no Monaco

Monaco is a DOM component and cannot render inside pi's TUI (`pi-tui` — ANSI differential renderer, not Ink, not blessed). Getting Monaco means a separate window (Glimpse native webview or a browser page over RPC / `pi-web-ui` fork). **Decision: no separate window.** Shiki is a tokenizer, not a renderer, so syntax highlighting works in the terminal. We give up Monaco's diff editor, mouse interaction, folding, search; keep everything in one terminal. Revisit if terminal line-comment UX proves too painful.

### D2 — Answers come from the main session with tools gated (option B)

Options considered:

| Option | Orchestrator context | Read-only guarantee | Context cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Side call via `@earendil-works/pi-ai`, zero tools | none | by construction | zero |
| B. Main session turn, tools gated | full | enforced by `tool_call` block | per question |
| C. Read-only child session with pumped context | briefed | by construction | isolated |

Use the alternate-screen renderer for application-owned scrolling (mouse, trackpad, keyboard); the main-screen renderer's scrollback will fight a diff view.

- `@earendil-works/pi-tui` — pane components
- `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` — `ExtensionAPI`, `DynamicBorder`
- `shiki` — `codeToTokens` (**not** `codeToANSI`, see R1)
- `simple-git` or `child_process` — commit list and diffs
- `parse-diff` or `gitdiff-parser` — hunk parsing
- `jsdiff` — intra-line word diff (`diffWordsWithSpace`) and comment re-anchoring
- `string-width`, `slice-ansi`, `strip-ansi`, `cli-truncate` — ANSI-safe width and slicing
- `tree-sitter` + `tree-sitter-java` — declaration boundaries; **or** a JVM sidecar using JavaParser / IntelliJ platform for real symbol resolution (decide in Phase 3a)
- `JClusterChanges` — partitioning; likely as a JVM sidecar

Issue #150: [P0][Roadmap] Qwen on M2: drive native decode toward 20–40 tok/s and speculative throughput toward 50–100 tok/s

## Overview

Drive the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Apple8 direct path on a 16 GB base M2 from ~2–2.5 tok/s native decode to a genuinely interactive local runtime. This is a performance program, not a promise of a specific token rate — continuously measure the hardware roofline and stop optimizing paths that cannot move the end-to-end token budget.

Target bands:

- **Native autoregressive decode:** 20–40 tok/s (stretch)
- **User-visible decode with MTP/speculation:** 50–100 tok/s (stretch)
- **Prefill/TTFT:** preserve large existing gains from direct Apple8 + MetalIO + prefix caching while decode is optimized

## Current validated baseline

The direct Apple8 runtime is model-output validated against the canonical-detile path on the M2.

### Prefill (direct raw Apple8 vs canonical-detile, fresh-process 63-token prompt)

- canonical TTFT: **165.645 s**; direct Apple8 TTFT: **11.738 s**; speedup: **14.11x**
- With 48/63-token prefix hit: canonical TTFT **44.264 s**; direct **3.644 s**; speedup **12.15x**; prefix restore ~**13–18 ms** for the process-local RAM tier

### Decode (the remaining problem)

Representative direct-path profiles show only **~2–2.5 tok/s**. A 2-token cached decode profile:

- wall: **970.7 ms / 2 tokens**
- routed expert requests: **320**; physical expert loads: **306**; expert cache hits: **14**
- expert I/O: **184.7 ms**; MoE: **421.0 ms**; GDN: **331.5 ms**; attention: **74.4 ms**; head: **52.1 ms**

Another direct run showed 320/320 routed expert loads for two tokens — essentially no useful decode residency.

Qwen's routed topology in these runs: top-k = **8**, roughly **20 routed MoE layers per token**, so about **160 routed expert applications per generated token**. The direct Apple8 path currently performs one expert operation at a time with synchronous GPU completion semantics — functionally correct but with huge dispatch/synchronization overhead.

## Hardware/roofline framing

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B activates ~3B parameters/token. Apple8 is ~4-bit-class storage plus per-row/group scale overhead → roughly **~1.5–1.7 GB of active weight data/token** if every active weight must be fetched from memory. On a base M2-class memory subsystem (~100 GB/s peak), the bandwidth-only ceiling is ~**60 tok/s** before accounting for GDN recurrent state, attention/KV traffic, router/top-k, dense/shared expert layers, lm_head, activations, Metal command submission/sync, cache misses/storage I/O, and imperfect bandwidth utilization.

Therefore:

- **50 tok/s native** means approaching the roofline extremely well
- **100 tok/s native** is not a credible default assumption for this model/hardware
- **50–100 tok/s user-visible** becomes much more plausible if MTP/speculative decoding yields >1 accepted token per expensive verification step

Keep this distinction visible in benchmarks and documentation.

## Use Cases / Performance strategy

### P0 — stop unnecessary expert loads

The old residency budget assumes ~**2 GB per expert slot**, but a raw direct Apple8 expert in the validated artifact is only about **1,671,168 bytes (~1.59 MiB)** before allocator/metadata overhead. Consequences:

1. previously produced pathological `resident cap=4 < topk=8` and exposed a real decode correctness bug;
2. still prevents the runtime from using available UMA for hot expert residency.

Replace the heuristic with target-native resident footprint accounting; experiment with materially larger caps (e.g. 16/32/48/64 where memory allows). Ultimately residency should be frequency/recency-aware rather than an equal-cap blind LRU. Goal: make MetalIO service the cold tail, not nearly every routed expert.

### P0 — fuse one routed MoE layer into a GPU wave

Current shape: per-expert load/wait → gate/up Metal work → wait → SwiGLU/down Metal work → wait → accumulate, i.e. ~**160 expert-level GPU interactions per token** at top-8 × ~20 routed layers. Target shape:

```text
router -> top-8
       -> acquire/pin/load required expert slots
       -> one Metal command buffer / layer
          - 8 gate/up projections
          - SwiGLU
          - 8 down projections
          - weighted reduction
       -> next layer
```

First milestone: reduce expert-level synchronization to roughly **one MoE synchronization per layer (~20/token)**. Later: encode multiple layers before host synchronization where dependencies permit.

### P0 — move Gated DeltaNet decode to Metal

Mandatory for the 50 tok/s program. Representative decode profiling shows **145–165 ms/token** in GDN alone; a 50 tok/s target has a total token budget of only **20 ms**, so 50 tok/s is mathematically impossible while GDN stays near its current cost. Implement a native Metal GDN decode path with recurrent state resident in UMA/GPU-visible memory, fusing input projections, causal convolution update, delta recurrence, gating/normalization, and output projection as practical.

## Execution tracker (from comments)

Instrument first:

- [ ] #156 — repeatable M2 Qwen decode roofline + synchronization benchmark: canonical baseline JSON before major decode changes; count host waits / command buffers / expert loads per token; reuse telemetry vocabulary from #148

P0 Milestones:

- [ ] #151 — target-native residency budgeting + hot expert policy: remove 2 GB/slot heuristic; normal M2 config should resolve to cap ≥ top-k when memory permits; drive physical expert loads/token down sharply
- [ ] #152 — fused top-k Apple8 MoE layer: depends on safe leases/transient slots from #151; target roughly one routed-MoE host synchronization per layer instead of per expert
- [ ] #153 — native Metal Gated DeltaNet decode: can proceed in parallel with #151/#152

## Milestone C verdict (falsified premise)

Milestone C (whole-token Metal, #154) sync-elimination premise is falsified on the M2. Measured bisect (commit 3cf7edd): whole-token kernel runs **75–80 ms per layer GPU** vs **4 ms per layer** for the per-layer path. Even a perfect whole-token kernel (~160 ms/token GPU) cannot beat the per-layer path (**161 ms/token wall**, CPU/GPU pipelined). **GPU compute is the bottleneck, not host syncs.** The whole-token path stays as a token-identical correctness reference (it caught the GQA rep=2 bug), default off.

Roadmap implication: decode speedups must come from faster kernels (fused MoE #152, native GDN #153), not fewer dispatches.

## Pain

Decode at ~2–2.5 tok/s is the blocker to interactive use; prefill is already 12–14x faster than the canonical path and must be preserved. GDN cost alone (145–165 ms/token) exceeds the entire 20 ms/token budget of a 50 tok/s target, and expert residency is effectively zero (306 physical loads for 320 requests over 2 tokens).

Issue #2909: [Problem] [Pi/OMP] Compiled OMP recursively spawns itself for ECC session-start hooks

## Overview

Under compiled Oh My Pi (OMP, a Bun-based binary), ECC's Pi adapter launches its `session_start` hook with `process.execPath`, which points to the `omp` binary instead of Node. This makes the hook spawn a recursive chain of OMP instances (`omp -> ECC session_start -> omp -> ...`), each re-initializing ECC and MCP integrations, resulting in high CPU/swap pressure, host unresponsiveness, and eventually `handler timed out after 30000ms` / `ECC session-start hook skipped`.

## Affected Environment

- ECC Pi adapter from merged PR #2759; ECC universal plugin loaded by OMP from its plugin directory
- OMP 18.0.11 (compiled binary), Node 26.7.0, Linux x86_64 (Arch-based), 20 logical CPUs
- Most visible with `omp --resume <session-id>` (Pi `session_start` lifecycle event with reason `resume`); new sessions can trigger the same path

## Root Cause

The adapter code in `.pi/extensions/index.ts`:

```ts
const child = execFile(
  process.execPath,
  [HOOK_RUNNER, spec.id, spec.script, spec.profiles],
  options,
  callback,
)
```

assumes the host executable is also a script runtime. Under compiled OMP the effective command becomes:

```text
omp .../ecc-universal/scripts/hooks/run-with-flags.js session:start ...
```

which starts another OMP instance that loads ECC and repeats the hook. Node-hosted Pi is unaffected. Notably, `process.release.name === "node"` alone is insufficient detection because compiled OMP reports `process.release.name = node`, `process.versions.bun = 1.4.0`, `process.execPath = .../omp`. The upstream adapter was tested only with Node/Pi on macOS; the compiled OMP/Bun case was not covered.

## Impact / Reproduction Data

Live reproduction on a 20-CPU Linux host: ~78 `omp` processes, ~290 `node-MainThread` processes, repeated `codebase-memory`, `node_repl`, and `chrome-devtools` descendants, load average >40. Killing only processes whose command line matched the recursive `run-with-flags.js session:start` invocation dropped load average to ~2.

Minimal comparison:
- `node run-with-flags.js session:start scripts/hooks/session-start.js minimal,standard,strict` — completes successfully
- `omp run-with-flags.js ...` — starts another OMP instance that repeats the hook

Diagnostic:

```js
console.log({
  releaseName: process.release?.name,
  bunVersion: process.versions?.bun,
  execPath: process.execPath,
})
```

## Expected Behavior

- Each ECC hook runs exactly once with a real Node runtime.
- Compiled OMP/Bun uses `node` or an explicit configured Node executable; Node-hosted Pi may keep `process.execPath`.
- Starting or resuming a session must never create another OMP process for the hook itself.

## Suggested Fix

Resolve the hook runtime independently of the host executable, e.g.:

```ts
const isNodeRuntime =
  process.release?.name === "node" &&
  !process.versions?.bun &&
  /^(?:node|nodejs)(?:\.exe)?$/i.test(path.basename(process.execPath))

const HOOK_RUNTIME =
  process.env.ECC_HOOK_NODE?.trim() ||
  (isNodeRuntime ? process.execPath : "node")
```

Requirements:
1. Never use compiled OMP's `process.execPath` as the hook interpreter.
2. Preserve `execFile` with a separate argv array and no shell.
3. Support an absolute `ECC_HOOK_NODE` override for installations where Node is not on `PATH`.
4. Add behavioral coverage for normal Node, compiled OMP/Bun, and the explicit override.

Secondary issue (separate from the runtime fix): the 30-second hook timeout equals OMP's 30-second lifecycle handler limit, leaving no timeout headroom.

## Out of Scope

No changes needed to Pi lifecycle registration, ECC hook stdin/stdout contracts, project working-directory resolution, profile gating, context injection, or shell-safety behavior.

## Resolution

Fixed in PR #2911: selects a real Node runtime for Pi hook execution under compiled OMP/Bun, preserves shell-free `execFile` invocation, adds `ECC_HOOK_NODE` override support, and includes regression tests/docs.

## Validation Evidence

A local installed-package workaround using the runtime guard was validated with:
- 27 adapter tests passing
- Fresh OMP startup smoke test with zero recursive `run-with-flags.js session:start` processes
- Direct hook completing under Node
- Original recursive pattern reproduced with compiled OMP before the guard was applied

Issue #93873: Windows process cancellation can leave reparented worker descendants alive

## Problem
Cancelling a local Windows background process through `tools.process_registry.ProcessRegistry.kill_process()` can report success while descendants survive after an intermediate wrapper exits.

The current Windows path delegates tree enumeration to `taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F`. `taskkill` can no longer discover a descendant after its intermediate parent has exited and the descendant has been reparented. Hermes then marks the session as killed while the surviving process is no longer tracked by the checkpoint.

## Reproduction
Executed on the real Windows host with a three-level chain:

```text
root.py  (sleeping; target of taskkill)
  └─ mid.py  (spawns grand.py, writes a completion marker, exits)
       └─ grand.py  (sleeping; reparented before root is killed)
```

After waiting for `mid.py` to exit, the real command returned:

- `taskkill /T /F` return code: `0`
- reparented grandchild after kill: alive
- repeated trials: `3/3` survivors

The session path nevertheless returned `{"status": "killed"}`.

The report's repository-wide claim that `CreateJobObject` was absent is outdated: `hermes_cli/process_identity.py` already uses a Job Object for backend lifetime. The defect remains because `tools/process_registry.py` did not create an independent Job Object per managed worker session.

## Root cause
PPID/taskkill tree traversal is not a durable ownership boundary after an intermediate process exits. The registry stored only the root PID and used a best-effort post-hoc tree walk, so orphaned descendants escaped both cancellation and later checkpoint recovery.

## Expected behavior
Each host-backed managed worker session must own its complete process tree independently of PPID changes. Cancelling the session must terminate the root and all descendants, including descendants reparented after an intermediate wrapper exits.

## Acceptance criteria
- Create a per-session Windows Job Object with `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`.
- Create the worker suspended, assign it to the Job Object before it can spawn descendants, then resume it.
- Use the Job Object for explicit cancellation and close it on terminal session cleanup.
- Retain a safe `taskkill` fallback for recovered sessions or hosts that reject nested jobs.
- Do not persist native handles in `processes.json`.

## Status

DESIGN INVESTIGATION — non-normative.

This issue records an emerging design for hierarchical Manager delegation, nested orchestration streams, and optional runtime reconciliation of the durable MORE coordination graph.

No SPEC change, runtime implementation, daemon, scanner, heartbeat, or automatic repair behavior is authorized by this issue. Promote only what prospective field evidence justifies.

## Motivation

IOC established that an **active Manager** should continue already-authorized internal orchestration across Executor and Reviewer handoffs until a genuine boundary. The subsequent field observation recorded in [Issue #12 comment 5231453905](https://github.com/JustAHobbyDev/more-agent-protocol/issues/12#issuecomment-5231453905) exposed a distinct topology problem:

- a cold-start work stream began with `[MANAGER → EXECUTOR]`;
- the Executor correctly completed its bounded task and returned `[EXECUTOR → MANAGER]`;
- no Manager execution context existed to consume that return;
- the Executor was correct not to promote itself into Manager or Reviewer authority.

The problem was therefore not an IOC violation by the Executor. The stream had been rooted one role too far downstream.

This raises a broader question: how should a Manager create independently orchestrated child streams that can themselves use IOC, survive session loss, return results correctly, and scale to concurrent/nested work without requiring Owner involvement for every decomposition?

## Current MORE compatibility

The current specification already appears to permit the basic shape:

- the Manager owns coordination and delegates bounded work;
- a separate issue is appropriate for genuinely independent parallel work;
- canonical handoff forms are not exhaustive; other addressed forms may be used where clear;
- every active MORE unit binds to exactly one governing GitHub work item;
- delegation cannot manufacture authority that the delegator does not possess.

The likely gap is therefore not whether Manager-to-Manager delegation is legal. It is the explicit semantics for **creating, returning, recovering, and reconciling nested Manager streams**.

## Proposed stream-root model

A continuously orchestrated root stream normally begins:

```text
[OWNER → MANAGER]
```

When Manager A creates an independently meaningful child stream B within authority already delegated to A, B may begin:

```text
[MANAGER → MANAGER]
```

Conceptually:

```text
Owner
  ↓
Manager A
  ├── Manager B
  │     ├── Executor
  │     └── Reviewer
  └── Manager C
        ├── Executor
        └── Reviewer
```

`A`, `B`, and `C` identify Manager instances/streams, not new MORE roles.

A fresh execution context bound to child work item B can therefore instantiate as Manager B and use ordinary IOC internally.

By contrast, `[MANAGER → EXECUTOR]` remains correct when an already-active Manager is delegating one bounded task and remains available to consume `[EXECUTOR → MANAGER]`. It is not sufficient by itself to establish a new independently orchestrated Manager-rooted stream.

## Authority-containment invariant

Manager delegation narrows or preserves existing authority; it does not create new Owner authority.

Conceptually:

```text
authority(child) ⊆ authority(parent)
```

If Manager A may investigate and prepare a candidate but may not deploy, Manager B cannot gain deployment authority merely because A created a child stream.

Loss of a delegator likewise never expands descendant authority.

## Delegation lineage

A child stream should need only a small durable parent reference, preferably:

- immediate parent work item;
- exact parent delegation/handoff when needed to identify the bounded authority;
- child objective, scope/exclusions, and delegated authority;
- return expectation.

The parent should durably record that the child stream exists and is an unresolved dependency.

This should use GitHub itself rather than a parallel task registry or transient status database.

Issue #664: [Task]: Run Skill scripts safely and preserve their results

## Overview

Eneo lacks a single runtime owner for executing a validated Skill script, enforcing per-turn cumulative cost limits, and preserving results after partial chat failures. This task introduces one concrete `SkillTurnExecution` module that owns the runtime contract — policy order, typed calls and outcomes, cumulative limits, evidence, and terminal cleanup — without connecting it to model-driven chat. It must fail safely under duplicate delivery, timeout, cancellation, invalid output, and storage failure.

Parent epic: #660. Depends on #661, #662, #663.

## Proposed approach

Add one `SkillTurnExecution` module that:
- owns policy order, typed calls and outcomes, cumulative limits, evidence, and terminal cleanup;
- opens one sandbox lazily, executes calls sequentially, rejects sibling calls that cannot fit within the remaining budget, and closes the sandbox once from the outer turn `finally`.

The sandbox seam is a narrow structural runtime Protocol for `open`, `execute`, and `close`, with one OpenSandbox adapter and one test fake. This is an external-service seam only — not a provider registry or plugin system.

Each call receives the actor, Question placeholder, frozen exact revision, validated script path, bounded arguments, and authorised current-turn input file keys. Before reading package bytes or opening the sandbox, `SkillTurnExecution` checks:
- the `Run Skill scripts` permission,
- parent-chat access,
- the live execution block,
- frozen manifest membership,
- remaining budget.

## Skill Script ABI v1

A closed ABI v1 defines the sandbox contract:

| Concern | Contract |
|---|---|
| Invocation | OpenSandbox receives `["python", "-E", "-s", "-B", "/skill/{script_path}", "--request", "/run/request.json", "--result", "/output/result.json"]` as an argv array. `-E` ignores Python environment variables, `-s` disables the user site, and no shell parses model-controlled values. |
| Filesystem | `/skill` and `/inputs` are read-only, `/run/request.json` is read-only, `/output` and bounded `/tmp` are writable, and the working directory is `/output`. |
| Request | `SkillScriptRequestV1` contains `version: 1`, a JSON-object `arguments` value capped at 16 KiB, 32 top-level keys, depth 8, and 2,000 nodes, plus an ordered input list of opaque key, guest path, verified media type, byte size, and content digest. |
| Result | The reserved `/output/result.json` contains `version: 1`, exactly one `text`, `json`, or `none` result kind, and an optional ordered list of relative output paths. Eneo does not persist the manifest as an attachment. |
| Diagnostics | Eneo drains stdout and stderr continuously, caps each at 32 KiB per call, discards bytes beyond the cap, and records only byte counts and truncation flags. Raw diagnostics never become model output or persisted evidence. |
| Completion | Exit `0` plus a valid result manifest is success. Non-zero exit is `script_failed`; timeout and resource exhaustion have separate typed outcomes; a missing or malformed manifest is `invalid_result`. Only success can admit files. |

## Per-turn ceilings (first release)

Fixed limits per turn:
- four script calls and evidence records,
- 60 CPU seconds,
- 120 wall-clock seconds,
- 50 MiB of current-turn input files,
- 64 KiB of serialized text or structured tool results,
- ten generated files,
- 50 MiB of generated file bytes.

The immutable Skill package is staged once per turn-scoped sandbox, not once per call. Package bytes follow #663's stored-package limits and do not consume the separate 50 MiB current-turn input ceiling. A single result contains exactly one bounded text value, bounded JSON value, or neither, plus optional admitted file references; JSON is limited to depth 16 and 10,000 nodes. These limits are code invariants; #661 may tighten them if its measured support envelope is lower.

## Generated artifact admission

After a zero exit status, the complete candidate output set is sent to one new generated-artifact admission entry point owned by `FileProtocol` and `FileService`. `GeneratedArtifactPolicyV1` does not change the declared-MIME semantics of normal user uploads and does not create a MIME policy in the Skill module. The fixed policy:

- accepts regular files only and derives type from bytes rather than script-supplied MIME;
- validates UTF-8 TXT and CSV, parses bounded JSON, and rejects NUL or extension mismatches;
- parses PDF to EOF, rejects encryption, JavaScript, launch actions, and embedded files, and serves accepted PDFs as downloads;
- validates DOCX and PPTX structure and limits, rejects macros, OLE or embedded packages, external relationships, encryption, traversal, decompression bombs, and mismatched content types, and serves accepted Office files as downloads;
- rejects images, XLSX, HTML, SVG, executables, general archives, polyglots, special files, and unknown formats.

## Idempotency and evidence

Bind each `tool_call_id` to a canonical request fingerprint covering the ABI profile, frozen revision ID and package digest, script path, canonical arguments JSON, and ordered input file IDs plus content digests. Reserve the call atomically in the Question-linked evidence envelope before opening a sandbox:

- the same call ID and fingerprint after completion replays the stored typed outcome without execution;
- the same call ID and fingerprint while running returns `script_execution_in_progress` without opening a second sandbox;
- the same call ID with another fingerprint returns `script_call_conflict` before package access or execution.

The Question placeholder owns one strict `SkillScriptExecutionEvidenceV1` with an ordered tuple of at most four body-free run records. Reserve and update each entry under a Question row lock or optimistic version check. The issue further extends the Question and File association with `tool_`-prefixed linkage (body truncated in source; exact remainder not specified).

## Pain

Without this module, no single component enforces total turn cost, safe sandbox execution, duplicate-delivery semantics, or evidence preservation across partial chat failures; scripts could run unboundedly, admit unsafe artifacts, or produce non-replayable, unaccountable results.

# [P0] Local approver principals, groups and policy-authorized decisions

## Overview

Approval authority is business authorization, not platform administration. This issue introduces one pluggable identity-resolution and authorization model for Talon approvals, built on a normalized internal principal. Parent: #147. Depends on #424 and policy schema #425. Integrates transactionally with #426. OIDC follow-up: #436.

Core v1 scope (settled): Talon-local authenticated human principals, revocable/rotatable one-time-issued bearer credentials, flat groups (no nesting, inheritance, or custom-role builder). Policy names one or more eligible approver groups; any one authenticated member of an eligible group may approve or reject. Decisions flow through the same resolver/authorization contract future OIDC will implement.

## Normalized principal model

```text
principal_id
subject
issuer
tenant scope
authentication method
credential/session id + version
assurance/provenance
groups
display metadata
active/revoked state
```

## Required identity separations

Record and keep distinct:

1. **agent identity** — AI use case presenting a Talon key;
2. **requester/runtime identity** — user/service/adapter requesting an operation, possibly client-asserted;
3. **approver identity** — authenticated human principal making the decision;
4. **admin/operator identity** — platform management authority.

Admin authority does not imply approver authority. Free-form `reviewed_by`, display names, emails, HTTP headers, workflow-supplied groups and fields are display/context metadata only and never authorize a decision.

## Identity boundary from session metadata (#401)

- `managed_by = talon|n8n|claude-code|codex|custom` is the only session lifecycle-manager field; it remains attribution and must never grant group membership, approval rights, admin rights or policy exemptions. Do not add or derive a separate `lifecycle_owner` field.
- Session `source = talon|client_asserted|vendor_asserted` records only how session identity was obtained; it does not establish lifecycle ownership or authenticate the manager.
- Approver resolution uses the canonical local/OIDC principal/group model, independent of session/client attribution. Reviewer/operator projections label asserted manager metadata honestly.
- Negative authorization tests must prove changing `X-Talon-Client` or `managed_by` cannot change approval per group.

## Authorization semantics

- Resolve required approver groups from the exact matched organization/agent approval rule captured by the approval subject. Organization-owned rule groups cannot be replaced by agent config or request metadata.
- Any one authenticated active principal in an allowed flat group may decide in v1.
- Decision authorization and pending-state transition are rechecked in one transaction/domain command; the authorization check occurs against the exact approval subject before committing.
- Expired, cancelled, invalidated or already-decided approvals cannot be decided again.
- Unauthorized attempts are denied, rate-limited and evidenced without changing approval state.
- Requester/approver comparison is recorded with identity assurance; no self-approval block in core v1 (deferred until requester identity is trustworthy across runtimes).
- System expiry/invalidation is a system actor/event, not a fake human decision.
- No permissive fallback when approval policy/groups are absent or unresolvable: creation/decision fails closed as a configuration error.
- The same normalized principal resolver and `authorizeDecision` path must authorize both `plan_review` and `action_execution`; neither implements a separate identity/group check. Approval type affects only the immutable subject and eligible-group policy supplied by the creating domain.
- Required negative cases: a principal authorized for plan reviews but not the action's captured group cannot decide the action approval; runtime/MCP/n8n context cannot introduce a new approval type or broaden eligible groups; an adapter cannot call a generic arbitrary approval-creation endpoint; local and future OIDC principals produce equivalent authorization decisions after normalization.

## Decision action contract

Authorized approvers may perform only two business decisions in core v1:

- `approve`
- `reject`

Rules:

- Approval comment optional and bounded; rejection reason required and bounded.
- Decision endpoints reject payload mutation fields: approvers cannot alter action arguments, destination, execution mode, operation ID, policy context or trusted catalog data. Material corrections require a new immutable operation with fresh evaluation/approval.
- A committed human decision is final: no `undo`, overwrite, or second human decision. Cancellation, system expiry, invalidation and outcome reconciliation are separate authorized/system actions with distinct evidence.

## Local identity lifecycle

CLI/config/API for:

- creating local human principals;
- one-time creation of revocable bearer credentials;
- rotating/revoking credentials;
- creating/deleting flat groups;
- assigning/removing group memberships;
- disabling/re-enabling principals;
- listing identities/credentials without exposing secrets/digests;
- recording authentication and authorization failures;
- preventing group deletion/redefinition from silently changing pending-approval authorization.

Pending approvals bind exact group requirement IDs/version/digest. A group/policy change invalidates pending requests under #425/#426 strict binding; committed decisions remain immutable history. Local user-facing configuration remains minimal: principal, credential, groups.

## Security requirements

- Tokens use at least 256 bits of CSPRNG entropy, shown exactly once; store token identifier plus secure verifier/digest (vault-backed allowed), never the raw bearer value.
- Token resolution and revocation use one shared long-lived repository/resolver, not a database opened inside each HTTP request.
- Constant-time verification where secret bytes are compared; database lookup behavior must not materially disclose valid token IDs.
- Explicit expiry optionality and created/last-used/revoked timestamps.
- Rotation is create-new + explicitly revoke-old, no accidental indefinite overlap.
- Decision endpoints have request-size bounds, rate limits and security evidence.
- Reviewer UI/API sessions never fall back to dev-open/admin authentication.
- Tenant scope derives from trusted principal configuration, not request body/header.
- Logs/evidence record credential ID/version — not key digest or token.

## Current implementation / Pain

Existing `internal/approver.Store` schema: `name`, `role`, `key_hash`, `created_at`. Deficiencies:

- generates a `talon_appr_` token with 12 random bytes (< 256 bits); stores a plain SHA-256 digest;
- no principal ID, tenant, groups, credential ID, expiry, revocation, rotation, disabled state or last-used audit;
- one `role` conflates identity membership and policy authorization;
- `DeleteByRole` deletes all credentials for a role instead of changing group membership;
- `List` exposes `key_hash` in its JSON record;
- `Resolve` returns raw `sql.ErrNoRows` and does not update usage metadata;
- opens its own SQLite connection via `NewStore(dbPath)`; the server's request resolver constructs/closes this store per approval resolution, causing avoidable connection/schema work and divergent resolver instances/semantics across CLI/API/UI paths.

Existing approval authorization paths are inconsistent: Plan Review has role/approval-chain logic tied to legacy compliance configuration; tool approval endpoints are admin-only and write identity as `admin_api`; the in-memory tool store accepts free-form `approvedBy`/`deniedBy` strings; some role logic defaults permissive.

A maintainer on the project repobuddy/repobuddy (unknown) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #594: merge-dep-prs: gate merges on verification reach covering blast radius

## What happened

A dependency PR bumped `changesets/action` v1 → v2.1.0 in `cyberuni/.github/.github/workflows/pnpm-release-changeset.yml`, the reusable release workflow that 30 repos call.

It was a *good* PR. It renamed the v2 inputs correctly (`version` → `version-script`, `publish` → `publish-script`, `commit` → `commit-message`, `GITHUB_TOKEN` env → `github-token` input) and left a comment explaining the npm 12 rationale. It passed every check in its own repo.

It also broke the release job in 25 downstream repos, because `changesets/action@v2` hard-refuses `@changesets/cli` v2:

```
Error: This version of the Changesets action is designed to work with Changesets CLI v3.
Changesets CLI v2 is not supported; use Changesets action v1 instead, which is compatible with CLI v2.
```

Each consumer stays green until its next push to `main`, then goes red one at a time. `cyberuni/universal-plugin` was the first to notice, days later, and only because trunk went red.

## The gap

`merge-dep-prs` uses **"CI is green"** as its merge oracle (§ Step 2 — Sort by CI status). Green is only evidence about what CI actually executed. The skill never asks what it executed.

Two independent quantities:

- **Blast radius** — what consumes the artifact this PR changes.
- **Verification reach** — what the green check actually ran.

Merging is safe when *reach ⊇ radius*. Otherwise green carries no information about the uncovered part.

A `.github` repo is the extreme case: reach is **zero** — it has no test suite because it has nothing to test locally, everything it ships executes elsewhere — while radius is 30 repos. The check is green by construction.

### Why this is not about major bumps

An earlier framing of this issue proposed gating on *major version bumps to consumed artifacts*. That is the wrong axis: semver is a property of the **dependency being bumped**, while the risk is a property of the **artifact being changed** and who executes it.

- **False negatives.** The same break lands without a major. A reusable workflow that changes an input default, a preset that tightens a rule, a package that narrows a peer range in a minor — consumers pin `@v2` / `main` / `^1` and get it regardless. In this incident the mechanism was a *runtime probe*: the action inspects the consumer's CLI version and refuses. A patch release that added that probe would have broken the same 25 repos.
- **False positives.** A major devDependency bump in a leaf repo with real local coverage has no blast radius and needs no gate.

### The same failure without a cross-repo boundary

This is not specific to `.github` repos or to multi-repo setups. Inside one monorepo:

Package A changes. CI runs `turbo run test --filter=...[origin/main]` (or `nx affected`, or a `paths:`-filtered job). Issue #726: HTMLElement.click() does not honor the click in progress flag

### Before you start

- [x] I searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate. (The closed stack-overflow issues are deep-DOM recursive traversal; this is re-entrant event dispatch.)
- [x] I tested against the latest release or `main`.
- [x] This is not a security vulnerability.

### obscura version or commit

v0.2.1 release binary and a source build at `f449e6fb3183138eb3e80f11fe44af31cefe0fae` (`main`)

### OS and architecture

Linux x86_64

### How are you using obscura?

CLI (fetch / serve / scrape / mcp)

### Affected area

JavaScript or DOM behavior

### Build variant

Render-enabled (--features render)

### Stealth mode

Off

### Reproduction

```
obscura fetch 'data:text/html,<button id=x>b</button>' --eval "(function(){ var n=0; var x=document.getElementById('x'); x.onclick=function(){ n++; if(n<5000) x.click(); }; x.click(); return n; })()"
```

`5000` is above the stack limit observed here, so the repro still reaches the swallowed `RangeError`, and it also caps execution on a build with a larger stack. Without the guard, recursion continues until stack exhaustion.

### Expected behavior

`1`. Per HTML, `click()` first returns for a disabled form control, then returns if the element's click in progress flag is set. Otherwise it sets the flag, fires a synthetic pointer event named `click`, and unsets the flag, so a handler that clicks its own element cannot re-enter. Headless Chrome returns `1`.

### Actual behavior

The command returned `2017` on this host on both v0.2.1 and `main`. The depth is stack-size dependent; without the guard, dispatch continues until stack exhaustion.

`click()` has no click in progress flag, so each dispatch re-enters until the stack runs out. The resulting `RangeError` is raised inside the listener, and `dispatchEvent` wraps every listener in `try { ... } catch(e) { console.error(e) }` (`bootstrap.js`, the inline-handler and registered-handler loops), so it is logged to stderr and does not propagate. The caller sees `click()` return normally: a `try`/`catch` around the outer `click()` catches nothing, and no `error` event or `window.onerror` fires. So one `click()` recurses to stack exhaustion, and the overflow surfaces only as a console trace.

### Does headless Chrome behave the same?

No. Chrome dispatches once.

### Additional context

Proposed fix and regression test: https://github.com/Vrejf/obscura/commit/495fadb

A `WeakSet` of elements with a click in progress, checked and set around the dispatch in `try`/`finally`. Behaviour verified against headless Chrome on the cases the guard could plausibly break:

| case | Chrome | stock | fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| handler clicks its own element | 1 | to stack exhaustion | 1 |
| three sequential clicks | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| flag clears after a listener throws | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| handler clicks a different element | fires both | fires both | fires both |
| mutual recursion, A clicks B clicks A | 2 | to stack exhaustion | 2 |

Also `cargo nextest run --release --features render --no-fail-fast` at 1493/1493. The obstacle course scores 32/33 on both the base and fixed commits, failing `observer-intersection` identically (`expected 'io:50', got ''`), so it is unrelated to this change.

The branch also carries fixes for #721 and #722. This commit touches only `bootstrap.js` and its test, so it is independent of both.
